title: The boy far from home
hook: Duleep Singh, still a child, is raised by British guardians and baptized a Christian

segments.voice: Yesterday, moh, and your line was taken away. What did you let go of, even for a minute? Today, the boy the diamond was taken from. Day nine hundred forty-one.

A garden by the Ganges at Fatehgarh, a long way from Lahore. A boy with a pony, a tutor, a few servants, and a Scottish doctor who has been put in charge of him. The boy has been a Maharaja. He has sat on his father's throne, been bowed to by generals, worn the jewels of the Punjab. Now he has lessons, a garden and guardians. His mother has been sent away, and the court he knew is gone. Today: the boy far from home.
screen: `A GARDEN AT FATEHGARH.` → `A BOY WHO WAS A MAHARAJA.` → `LESSONS, AND GUARDIANS.`

segments.voice: First, the guardian. After the annexation, Duleep Singh was placed in the care of Dr. John Login, who had looked after the treasury at Lahore. Login and his wife, Lena, raised him. Her later book about the boy is warm toward him, and also plainly written from the guardians' side. Second, the move. The boy was taken out of the Punjab to Fatehgarh, away from the Sikh court, the gurdwaras of Lahore and anyone who might raise him as a Sikh king. The British saw a boy who could become a rallying point. So they kept him far away. Third, the baptism. In those years, while still a boy in his early teens, Duleep Singh asked to become a Christian, and he was baptized. The Login account says the wish was his own, that he'd been listening to a household servant read from the Bible. Some Sikh writers see it differently: a child cut off from his mother, his faith and his people, who was shaped by the only adults left around him. Both readings are still held, and the sources can't fully settle what was in a child's heart. Fourth, what Sikh scripture offers a lonely child. In a hymn of Guru Arjan in Raag Bilaval, in the Guru Granth Sahib, the Guru says the hot wind does not touch the one who shelters in the Lord: a protecting line is drawn on every side, and no pain comes near. Those words were there, in the scripture of the faith he was raised away from. That's today's line.
screen: `DR. LOGIN, THE GUARDIAN.` · `TAKEN OUT OF THE PUNJAB.` · `A CHILD IS BAPTIZED.` · `THE HOT WIND DOES NOT TOUCH.` · then, large: `A BOY FAR AWAY.`

segments.voice: Two minutes for a child far from home. Sit, and let your breathing slow. Go back to a night when you were young and away from home: a sleepover, a hospital bed, a camp, a new house. Remember the room, the sounds, the strange bed. Now remember what helped, if anything did: a voice, a light left on, something from home in your hands. Hold that small thing in mind. Then let a child who is far from home today come to mind, and wish them that same small thing. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Sarnai, sanctuary or shelter, where the hot wind cannot touch the one within: Duleep Singh, a Maharaja no longer, raised by British guardians at Fatehgarh. Today's word.
Your line: a boy far away. Today, think of one child far from home, and do one small thing that reaches toward a child near you. Day nine hundred forty-one.

howItsDone: Sikh histories tell Duleep Singh's childhood under British guardianship as part of the loss of the kingdom, and his baptism is read differently in different accounts: as his own choice, or as the result of being separated from his mother and his faith.

fork.setup: you're a British official after the annexation. the boy Maharaja could become a rallying point. what do you do, as the histories tell it?
options: leave him at Lahore with his court.
move him far away, under a British guardian.
send him to live with his mother.
fork.reveal: he was taken to Fatehgarh under Dr. Login, far from the Punjab and his mother.

Editor: practice rewritten around the listener's own memory of a night away from home, since the old version (holding a child in mind with warmth) repeated days 928 and 936.
Login 'had looked after the treasury at Lahore' (the toshakhana) — confirm.
'Lena' Login: confirm the first name of Lady Login (Lena Campbell Login).
The household servant reading the Bible (Bhajan Lal in the Login account) is unnamed; confirm.
'Some Sikh writers see it differently' is a general characterization of later Sikh historiography; a Keeper may want it softened to 'Sikh writers'.
Guru Arjan's hymn (tu mera pita tu hai mera mata...) paraphrased; confirm Ang 103 and Gurmukhi ਮਾਤਾ.

Audit: Guru Arjan's 'you are my father, you are my mother' (Ang 103) was already used on day 928; replaced with Bilaval M5, Ang 819 (taatee vaao na lagaee paarbrahm sharnaaee); confirm Ang and Gurmukhi ਸਰਣਾਈ. 'Still a child' changed to 'a boy in his early teens' (baptism usually dated 1853, at about 14).
